subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The DARPA Grand Challenge
description: A 60-second lesson on The DARPA Grand Challenge.

hook.text: In 2004, the US military offered a million-dollar prize for a robot car that could cross a desert.

buildup.text: Fifteen vehicles entered the DARPA Grand Challenge. Not one finished the 142-mile course.

discovery.text: The best car made it just seven miles before crashing into a boulder and catching fire.

twist.text: One year later, five cars finished the course—Stanford's Stanley won in under seven hours.

climax.text: The challenge proved autonomous driving was possible and launched an entire industry overnight.

punchline.text: A desert race nobody could finish birthed self-driving cars.

quiz.question: How many vehicles finished the first DARPA Grand Challenge in 2004?

details.summary: DARPA's Grand Challenges in 2004 and 2005 offered million-dollar prizes for autonomous vehicles completing desert courses, with Stanford's Stanley winning in 2005 and launching the modern self-driving car industry.
details.whyItMatters: The DARPA Grand Challenge proved that autonomous vehicles could navigate real-world terrain. Most leaders of today's AV industry, including Waymo's founders, participated in these competitions.
takeaways: No vehicle finished the 2004 desert course successfully
Stanford's Stanley won the 2005 desert challenge
The 2007 Urban Challenge tackled city driving for the first time

faq.question: Why did DARPA sponsor autonomous vehicle competitions?
faq.answer: Congress mandated that one-third of military ground vehicles be autonomous by 2015. DARPA used prize competitions to accelerate research, correctly betting that competition would advance the technology faster than grants.

faq.question: How did the DARPA challenges lead to today's self-driving car industry?
faq.answer: Many challenge participants went on to found or lead AV companies. Sebastian Thrun started Google's self-driving project, Chris Urmson co-founded Aurora, and Bryan Salesky founded Argo AI.
